lec06kp01-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p1-bridge.text: Weeks 2 to 4: fully connected layers, learned weights, and the risk of overfitting. This week the data are photographs: how should they enter a network?

lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p1|Three week cards: Week 2 fully connected layer, Week 3 backpropagation and gradient descent learn the weights, Week 4 too many weights invite overfitting; on the right a 4×4 image with 16 pixels and the questions what to keep and how many weights; bottom strip KP01 (this unit), KP02 (self-study), KP03, KP04, KP05–KP07, KP08–KP09, KP10 (self-study), Week 7 classics.

lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-16.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p1#16
lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-16.text: This week: the data are photographs

lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-44.name: term:fully connected layer
lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-44.text:
Fully connected layer:
every output sees
every input

lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-45.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p1#45
lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-45.text:
Backpropagation and
gradient descent
learn the weights

lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-48.name: term:pixel
lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-48.text:
Pixel: one cell of
an image, storing one
brightness number.

lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-49.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p1#49
lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-49.text:
How should a photograph enter a network, so that the most
important information is kept and the weights stay trainable?

lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-62.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p1#62
lec06kp01-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp01-p1-62.text: This week starts here: KP01 compares one long vector with scanning the image by a small set of weights.

lec06kp01-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p2-bridge.text: Photographs enter a fully connected layer as one long vector. Once the $4\times4$ grid is flattened, are neighbours still next to each other?

lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p2|4×4 grid numbered 0 to 15, cell 4p+q; cell 5 (orange) with neighbours 1, 9, 4, 6 (blue); flattened 16-cell strip: left and right neighbours 1 apart, up and down 4 apart; cell 3 (red) next to cell 4 in the strip.

lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-64.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p2#64
lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-64.text: Fully connected layer: every output sees every input, one weight per link.

lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-65.name: term:flatten
lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-65.text: Flatten: lay the $H\times W$ grid out row after row as a vector of length $HW$.

lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-66.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p2#66
lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-66.text: $I[p,q]$: the pixel at row $p$, column $q$ (from $0$); after flattening it sits at position $4p+q$.

lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-69.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p2#69
lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-69.text:
Cell $3$ ends row $0$, cell $4$ starts row $1$: far apart in the image,
side by side in the strip.

lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-89.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p2#89
lec06kp01-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp01-p2-89.text: After flattening: left-right $1$ apart, up-down $4$ apart, and cells $3$, $4$ side by side.

lec06kp01-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec06kp01-u01-p3-title.text: A dense layer cannot see neighbours

lec06kp01-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p3-bridge.text: Flattening splits up-down neighbours: they end up far apart in the long vector, yet none of the $16$ numbers is lost. Where is the problem?

lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p3|Top: the original 16-cell strip, each cell with weight w0 to w15; bottom: the cells shuffled with their weights, cells 5, 1, 9, 4, 6 linked to their new places; both outputs y=Σ w_t x_t are equal; cost 1: the same edge must be learned at each position; cost 2: weights = inputs × outputs; common error: a perceptron on flattened images can still read digits.

lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-119.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p3#119
lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-119.text: Each cell moves together with its weight $w_t$ ($x_t$ is the value of cell $t$); the sum is unchanged, so the layer never uses which cells are neighbours.

lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-120.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p3#120
lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-120.text:
The same edge at different
positions must be learned again
with different weights.

lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-121.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p3#121
lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-121.text:
Number of weights $=$ inputs $\times$
outputs, huge for a large image.

lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-122.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p3#122
lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-122.text:
Thinking a multilayer perceptron on
flattened images can never read digits.
It can, but with many weights.

lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-123.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p3#123
lec06kp01-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp01-p3-123.text: Flattening loses no numbers; the fully connected layer treats all positions alike and cannot see neighbours.

lec06kp01-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p4-bridge.text: The fully connected layer treats all positions alike and cannot see neighbours. If we do not flatten and compute on the original grid, how does it work?

lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p4|Formula s[i,j]=ΣΣ I[i+m,j+n]K[m,n], p=i+m, q=j+n; two placements of a 3×3 kernel on a 5×5 image (orange, blue), moved right by one; the two matching cells of the 3×3 feature map; 5-3+1=3 positions per direction; terms: kernel (filter), feature map, valid output, ★.

lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-51.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p4#51
lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-51.text: $m,n$ sweep the kernel; $(i,j)$ is the output at the kernel's top-left corner.

lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-55.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p4#55
lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-55.text: only $5-3+1=3$ positions per direction, so the feature map is $3\times3$

lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-56.name: term:kernel
lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-56.text:
Kernel (or filter): a small $k\times k$ grid of
weights; multiply aligned cells, add them up.

lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-57.name: term:feature map
lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-57.text:
Feature map: the numbers from every kernel
position, arranged by position.

lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-58.name: term:valid output
lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-58.text:
Valid output: outputs from positions where
the kernel lies fully inside the image.

lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-59.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p4#59
lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-59.text:
$\star$: the symbol for this sliding
multiply-and-add, named in KP04.

lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-60.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p4#60
lec06kp01-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp01-p4-60.text: Align the kernel's corner with $(i,j)$, multiply and add: one cell; slide it everywhere: the whole map.

lec06kp01-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec06kp01-u01-p5-title.text: Checkerboard: 5 on a match, 0 beside it

lec06kp01-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p5-bridge.text: Align the kernel, multiply and add: one cell of the feature map. With the main example plugged in, what is each cell?

lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p5|5×5 checkerboard I (1 where p+q is even) ★ kernel K (1 at the corners and centre) = feature map s; s[0,0]=I[0,0]+I[0,2]+I[1,1]+I[2,0]+I[2,2]=1+1+1+1+1=5; s[0,1]=0; rows [5,0,5], [0,5,0], [5,0,5]; definitions of convolutional neural network and convolutional layer.

lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-103.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p5#103
lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-103.text:
Of the nine products only the five where the
kernel is $1$ are nonzero, and those five
image cells are all $1$.

lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-104.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p5#104
lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-104.text:
Move the window right by one: the five $1$s
all land on $0$s, so $s[0,1]=0$.

lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-105.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p5#105
lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-105.text: The kernel detects a pattern: largest on a match.

lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-107.name: term:convolutional neural network
lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-107.text: Convolutional neural network: a network built mainly from this operation.

lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-108.name: term:convolutional layer
lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-108.text: Convolutional layer: a layer that does it.

lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-109.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p5#109
lec06kp01-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp01-p5-109.text: A checkerboard with a five-ones kernel: $5$ where the pattern matches, $0$ one cell further.

lec06kp01-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p6-bridge.text: A convolutional layer slides one small kernel to make the feature map; how much does that save? Fix the task first: input and output both $4\times4$. How do the windows at the border connect?

lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p6|Pixels per output on a 4×4 grid: rows [4,6,6,4], [6,9,9,6], [6,9,9,6], [4,6,6,4]; three sample windows: corner 4, edge 6, inside 9, faint red cells outside the image get no connection; 4×4+8×6+4×9=16+48+36=100 connections; definitions of same-size output and connection.

lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-98.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p6#98
lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-98.text: Three sample windows (centred on their output)

lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-102.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p6#102
lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-102.text: Faint red cells lie outside the image and get no connection; filling the border is left to KP07.

lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-103.name: term:same-size output
lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-103.text: Same-size output: a $4\times4$ input and a $4\times4$ output, one output per pixel position.

lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-104.name: term:connection
lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-104.text: Connection: one path from an input pixel into an output, multiplied by one weight.

lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-106.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p6#106
lec06kp01-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp01-p6-106.text: With a same-size output each $3\times3$ window connects only to real pixels: corners $4$, edges $6$, inside $9$, $100$ connections.

lec06kp01-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p7-bridge.text: With a same-size output each window connects only to real pixels: $100$ connections. How many weights does a fully connected layer need, and how many are left with one shared kernel?

lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p7|Three bars: fully connected 256 (red), neighbours only 100 (yellow), neighbours with sharing 9 (green); arrows: sparse connectivity 256→100, parameter sharing 100→9; 4×4 input, 4×4 output, no bias; a convolutional layer is a fully connected layer with two restrictions; common error: after sharing still 100 connections sharing 9 numbers.

lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-28.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p7#28
lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-28.text: Bar length: different weights ($4\times4$ in, $4\times4$ out, no bias)

lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-29.name: term:sparse connectivity
lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-29.text:
Sparse connectivity: each output connects
only to a small nearby patch; all other
connections are absent. $256\to100$

lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-30.name: term:parameter sharing
lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-30.text:
Parameter sharing: every position uses
the same kernel weights. $100\to9$

lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-31.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p7#31
lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-31.text:
A convolutional layer is a fully connected
layer with these two restrictions.

lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-32.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p7#32
lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-32.text:
Common error: confusing
connections with weights.

lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-33.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p7#33
lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-33.text:
After sharing: still $100$ connections,
sharing $9$ numbers.

lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-34.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p7#34
lec06kp01-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp01-p7-34.text: Sparse connectivity cuts $256$ weights to $100$, and parameter sharing cuts $100$ to $9$.

lec06kp01-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p8-bridge.text: Sparse connectivity and parameter sharing cut $256$ weights to $9$ on the $4\times4$ example. Why is this saving allowed, and how big is the gap for larger images?

lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p8|Left: inductive bias (an assumption put in before seeing data, a strong prior); useful patterns are local → sparse connectivity; the same pattern can appear anywhere → parameter sharing; fewer weights, lower overfitting risk. Right: 28×28 grayscale to 512 units 784×512=401,408; 224×224×3=150,528 numbers to 512 units 77,070,336; 64 kernels of 3×3×3 64×27=1,728, independent of image size; Added: outputs differ in size, do not divide.

lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-20.name: term:inductive bias
lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-20.text:
Inductive bias: an assumption put into the model
before it sees data; a very strong prior.

lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-22.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p8#22
lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-22.text:
the same pattern can appear
anywhere with the same meaning

lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-23.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p8#23
lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-23.text:
Photographs roughly satisfy both, so few weights suffice;
fewer weights also lower the overfitting risk of Week 4.

lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-28.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p8#28
lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-28.text:
$64$ kernels of $3\times3\times3$ (the last $3$ is
the $3$ colour numbers of each pixel)

lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-30.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p8#30
lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-30.text: The convolutional count does not depend on the image size.

lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-31.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p8#31
lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-31.text: The outputs differ in size, so do not divide the two.

lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-32.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p8#32
lec06kp01-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp01-p8-32.text: The two restrictions are assumptions about photographs; $64$ kernels need only $1{,}728$ weights, whatever the image size.

lec06kp01-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec06kp01-u01-p9-title.text: Shift the input, the output shifts too

lec06kp01-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p9-bridge.text: Parameter sharing keeps the weight count size-free: one kernel, whatever the image size. Besides saving weights, what else does it bring?

lec06kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp01-p9-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p9|Four rows: input [0,2,1,3,0,0], shifted [0,0,2,1,3,0], output [10,13,19,12,0], new output [0,10,13,19,12], arrows show the shift by one; the red cell is a new border value; s[t]=x[t]w[0]+x[t+1]w[1] (Added), w=[4,5], s[1]=2·4+1·5=13; definition of translation equivariance.

lec06kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp01-p9-71.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p9#71
lec06kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp01-p9-71.text: red cell: a new value at the border

lec06kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp01-p9-74.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p9#74
lec06kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp01-p9-74.text:
Every output uses the same kernel and looks
only at the numbers in its window, not at
where the window is: the same pattern gives
the same numbers wherever it moves.

lec06kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp01-p9-75.name: term:translation equivariance
lec06kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp01-p9-75.text:
Translation equivariance: when the
input shifts, the output shifts equally.

lec06kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp01-p9-76.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p9#76
lec06kp01-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp01-p9-76.text: Shift the input right by one and $10,13,19,12$ shift right by one too: translation equivariance.

lec06kp01-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec06kp01-u01-p10-bridge.text: Shift the input right by one and the output shifts right by one too. Does that mean the output did not change? What does the red border cell tell us?

lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-1.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p10|Left: translation equivariance (a convolutional layer has it): output [10,13,19,12,0] becomes [0,10,13,19,12], the red cell is a new border value; right: translation invariance (not a convolutional layer alone): the output does not move; pooling gives only local approximate invariance; Added: conditions stride 1 and away from the border; next KP02 LeNet, KP03 one layer taken apart.

lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-24.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p10#24
lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-24.text: Invariant: not a convolutional layer alone

lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-40.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p10#40
lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-40.text:
The output moves right by one cell. The red cell is a
new border value: positions too close to the border
do not follow equivariance.

lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-41.name: term:translation invariance
lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-41.text:
Translation invariance: when the input shifts,
the output does not change at all.

lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-42.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p10#42
lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-42.text:
Equivariance means moving along; invariance
means not moving at all. They differ.

lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-43.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p10#43
lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-43.text:
Pooling, in KP08–KP09, brings only approximate
invariance to small shifts, and only locally.

lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-44.name: term:stride
lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-44.text: Conditions: the kernel moves one cell at a time (a stride of $1$), away from the border; KP06 looks closer.

lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-45.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p10#45
lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-45.text: Next: what network do we build? KP02 looks at LeNet, KP03 takes one convolutional layer apart.

lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-46.name: fig:lec06-kp01-p10#46
lec06kp01-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp01-p10-46.text: Equivariance means the output moves with the input, not that it stays still; it needs a stride of $1$, away from the border.

lec06kp01-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge

steps.label: Flatten vs. scan
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate. Made from the confirmed lecture lec06-kp01: the pages were planned first, each page is mainly one native infographic, and terms are defined on the page where they are used. 11 main pages that open Week 6, plus 2 extension pages (upper bound on connections, exercises) that are not timed. Content marked Added is not in the course source and was added by the lecture. The exercise page gives hints only, no answers.

steps.label: Opening
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP01 and of Week 6. Two prerequisites: the fully connected layer of Week 2, where every output connects to every input with one weight per connection; and the idea of Week 3 that weights are learned, by computing gradients with backpropagation and adjusting them with gradient descent. Let us spend a minute on the three weeks. In Week 2 we stacked fully connected layers into a multilayer perceptron; in Week 3 we learned to train it; in Week 4 we saw that with many weights a model tends to memorise the training data, which is overfitting. This week the data are photographs. On the right is the smallest example, a 4 by 4 image with 16 pixels; a pixel is one cell of the image and stores one brightness number. The question has two halves: what information must be kept, and whether the weights become too many to train. The strip at the bottom is only a map of the week: KP01 is this unit, KP02 and KP10 are self-study, and classic architectures are left to Week 7. We start with the most direct approach. Next, the next page covers flattening.

steps.label: Flattening
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the opening. A fully connected layer needs a vector, so the most direct approach is to flatten: lay the grid out row after row as a vector whose length is height times width. We name a pixel by row p and column q, counting from 0; after flattening a 4 by 4 image it sits at position 4p plus q. The lecture added this formula, hence the Added chip. Look at the orange cell 5: its neighbours above, below, left and right are the blue 1, 9, 4 and 6. After flattening, the left and right neighbours 4 and 6 still sit next to 5, 1 apart; but the upper and lower neighbours 1 and 9 are each 4 apart, exactly the length of a row. Now the red cell 3: it ends row 0, and cell 4 starts row 1; far apart in the image, side by side in the strip. Next, the next page covers how a fully connected layer treats positions.

steps.label: Positions alike
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on flattening. Flattening itself loses no numbers; the problem is the fully connected layer. The top row is the original strip, and below each cell hangs the weight w that connects to it; the bottom row shuffles the cells, but each cell carries its own weight along. The output multiplies each value by its weight and adds everything; addition ignores order, so both rows give exactly the same result. The lecture added this shuffling argument. So a fully connected layer never uses which cells are neighbours: for it, the fact that cells 5 and 9 are upper and lower neighbours does not exist. That has two costs. First, the same edge at different positions must be learned again with different weights. Second, the number of weights is inputs times outputs, huge for a large image. And one common error: a multilayer perceptron on flattened images can still recognise handwritten digits; it just needs many weights and learns local patterns the hard way. Next, the next page covers the sliding multiply-and-add.

steps.label: Sliding
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on how a fully connected layer treats positions. The other way is not to flatten. Prepare a small set of weights arranged as a k by k grid, called a kernel, also called a filter. Lay it over a small patch, multiply the aligned cells and add everything up: one number. Move the kernel one cell right or down and compute again. These numbers, arranged by position, form a new grid called the feature map. The formula: s at i, j equals the sum over m and n from 0 to k minus 1 of I at i plus m, j plus n, times K at m, n. Here i, j is the output position where the kernel's top-left corner sits; m and n only sweep the cells of the kernel; the pixel used is at row i plus m, column j plus n, the p and q from before. The kernel must lie fully inside the image; such an output is a valid output. A 5 by 5 image with a 3 by 3 kernel has only 5 minus 3 plus 1, that is 3 positions per direction, so the feature map is 3 by 3. The star in the figures stands for this sliding multiply-and-add; KP04 names it formally. Next, the next page covers the checkerboard example.

steps.label: Checkerboard
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the sliding multiply-and-add. The main example is a 5 by 5 checkerboard: the pixel at row p, column q is 1 when p plus q is even and 0 otherwise. The kernel has 1 at its four corners and its centre and 0 elsewhere. Look at the framed window at the top left: the five 1s of the kernel all land on 1s of the image. Of the nine products only the five where the kernel is 1 are nonzero, so s at 0, 0 is the sum of I at 0 0, 0 2, 1 1, 2 0 and 2 2: 1 plus 1 plus 1 plus 1 plus 1 equals 5. Move the window one cell right and the five 1s all land on 0s, so s at 0, 1 is 0. The whole feature map has rows 5 0 5, 0 5 0 and 5 0 5. The kernel acts as a pattern detector: the output is largest where the pattern in the window matches it. A network built mainly from this operation is a convolutional neural network, and a layer that does it is a convolutional layer. Compared with a fully connected layer, how much does it save? Next, the next page covers the fair comparison.

steps.label: Fair comparison
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the checkerboard example. For a fair comparison we fix one task: a 4 by 4 input and a 4 by 4 output, one output per pixel position; this is a same-size output. Earlier the window was aligned by its top-left corner and gave only the valid output, which is smaller; here, to keep the output as large as the input, each output's 3 by 3 window is centred on its own position. Near the border part of the window falls outside the image, the faint red part, and it gets no connection. The lecture added this centred setting; filling the border is left to KP07. A connection is one path from an input pixel into an output, multiplied by one weight. Count them: the four corners connect to 4 each, the other 8 border positions to 6 each, and the 4 inner positions to 9 each, so 16 plus 48 plus 36 equals 100 connections. Next, the next page covers the two restrictions.

steps.label: Two restrictions
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the fair comparison. The three bars are three layers for the same 4 by 4 task. Fully connected: every output connects to all 16 cells, 16 times 16 equals 256 connections with one weight each, so 256 weights. Neighbours only: 100 connections, each still with its own weight, so 100. Neighbours only with sharing: all outputs share one 3 by 3 kernel; there are still 100 connections but only 9 different numbers, so 9 weights. None of these counts includes biases, a convention the lecture added. Each restriction has a name. Letting every output connect only to a small nearby patch, with all other connections absent, is sparse connectivity; it cuts 256 to 100. Using the same kernel weights everywhere is parameter sharing; it cuts 100 to 9. This is the key of the unit: a convolutional layer is a fully connected layer with these two restrictions, not a different kind of mathematics. A common error is to confuse connections with weights: after sharing there are still 100 connections; they just share 9 numbers. Next, the next page covers inductive bias and large images.

steps.label: Inductive bias
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the two restrictions. These two restrictions are also assumptions put into the model before it sees any data; such an assumption is an inductive bias, and it can be seen as a very strong prior. Sparse connectivity assumes that useful patterns are local; parameter sharing assumes that the same pattern can appear anywhere with the same meaning. Photographs roughly satisfy both, so the model can learn with few weights, and fewer weights also lower the overfitting risk of Week 4. On the right are weight counts for larger images. A 28 by 28 grayscale digit connected to 512 units needs 784 times 512, that is 401,408 weights. A 224 by 224 colour photograph has 3 colour numbers per pixel, 150,528 numbers, and connecting it to 512 units takes 77,070,336. With 64 kernels of 3 by 3 by 3, where the last 3 stands for the 3 colour numbers of each pixel, only 64 times 27, that is 1,728 weights are needed, whatever the image size. But the two layers have outputs of different sizes, so do not divide these numbers; the lecture added this caution, and the fair comparison is the same-size 4 by 4 example. Next, the next page covers translation equivariance.

steps.label: Equivariance
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on inductive bias and large images. Take the simplest 1-D example. The signal x sits on a row of 6 cells: 0, 2, 1, 3, 0, 0; the kernel w is 4, 5. The 1-D sliding multiply-and-add is s at t equals x at t times w at 0, plus x at t plus 1 times w at 1; the lecture added this 1-D form. The output is 10, 13, 19, 12, 0; for example s at 1 equals 2 times 4 plus 1 times 5, which is 13. Shift the whole input right by one cell, to 0, 0, 2, 1, 3, 0, and the output is 0, 10, 13, 19, 12: the old outputs 10, 13, 19, 12 have shifted right by one cell as a whole. The red 0 on the left is a new value at the border, and the old 0 on the right is pushed out. Why? Every output uses the same kernel, and the computation looks only at the numbers in the window, not at where the window is; so wherever the same pattern moves, the same numbers are computed there. This property is translation equivariance: when the input shifts by some amount, the output shifts by the same amount. Next, the next page covers equivariance versus invariance.

steps.label: Not invariance
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on translation equivariance. Translation equivariance does not mean the output stays the same. On the left is the equivariance a convolutional layer has: the input shifts right and the outputs 10, 13, 19, 12 shift with it. On the right is translation invariance: when the input shifts, the output does not change at all; a convolutional layer alone does not have this. Pooling, introduced in KP08 to KP09, brings only approximate invariance to small shifts, and only locally. Equivariance also has conditions, which the lecture added: the kernel moves one cell at a time, which KP07 calls a stride of 1, and only positions far enough from the border count. The red cell on the left does not satisfy this; it is a new value at the border. KP06 looks at this more carefully. We now know the benefits of not flattening, connecting only neighbours and sharing weights; what network do we actually build? KP02 gives the first complete example with LeNet, and KP03 takes one convolutional layer apart. Next, the next page covers the summary and misconceptions.

steps.label: Summary
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on equivariance versus invariance. One sentence to keep: a fully connected layer on a flattened image cannot tell which pixels are neighbours and must learn one weight per connection; a convolutional layer connects only neighbours, which is sparse connectivity, and shares one kernel over the whole image, which is parameter sharing, so it has far fewer weights, and its feature map shifts when the input shifts, which is translation equivariance. The top row has three formulas: the sliding multiply-and-add, with a valid output of size height minus k plus 1 by width minus k plus 1; with a same-size output, a fully connected layer has height times width squared weights and a convolution only k squared, 256, 100 and 9 for 4 by 4; and translation equivariance, shifting then computing equals computing then shifting, for a stride of 1 away from the border. The bottom row lists four misconceptions: a perceptron on flattened images can in fact recognise images; a convolutional layer is a fully connected layer with two restrictions; after sharing there are still 100 connections; equivariant means moving along, invariant means not moving at all. Next, the next page covers the extension on the upper bound.

steps.label: Extension: bound
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the summary and misconceptions. This is an extension page, not timed, and its content was added by the lecture. With a same-size output and a k by k window, if every window were complete, each output would connect to k squared pixels, giving height times width times k squared connections; this is the upper bound. For 4 by 4 with a 3 by 3 window that is 4 times 4 times 9, which is 144. In fact the border windows reach outside the image and that part is not connected, so there are only 100, which is 44 fewer. The larger the image, the smaller the share of the border, and the closer the actual count gets to the bound. KP05 writes sparse connectivity and parameter sharing as general counting formulas. Next, the next page covers the extension exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the extension on the upper bound. This is an extension page, not timed. All four exercises give hints only; compute first. Exercise 1: input and output are both 8 by 8 with a 3 by 3 window; count the weights of the three layers; the hint is to count the corners, the other border positions and the inner positions separately for neighbours only. Exercise 2 was added by the lecture: flatten a 5 by 5 image, find where a cell and its upper and lower neighbours go, and list the pairs that are adjacent in the strip but at the two ends of two rows; the hint is that the ends are the right end of row p and the left end of row p plus 1, each put into 5p plus q. Exercise 3 is also added: a 4 by 4 image with a 2 by 2 kernel; compute the 3 by 3 feature map by sliding multiply-and-add; the hint is that only two kernel cells are 1, so each cell adds two pixels. Exercise 4: a 1-D signal with the kernel 1, minus 1, computed before and after a shift by one; the hint is to write the formula for s at t first and then compare where the nonzero values are. That ends KP01; KP02 is self-study on the first successful example, LeNet, and the class continues with KP03.
